response: ## The finding ``` crime_00037 · oversized_raster · "Oversized Raster" · severity: low · confidence: 0.95 src/assets/hero-banner.png byte size: 260,000 bytes (253.9 KB) severity ladder: low ≥ 200 KB · medium ≥ 500 KB · high ≥ 1000 KB format: png ``` 253.9 KB, sitting just over the bottom rung of the ladder (200 KB) and nowhere near medium (500 KB). ## Verdict: request changes, don't block Not a blocker. It's the lowest-scoring finding in the whole report (`agent_risk` 0.14, `severity` 0.4), the effort is `quick`, and the fix is confined to one file with no code changes. Blocking a PR on a 254 KB asset that's 1.27× the advisory threshold would be disproportionate — nothing downstream is wrong, the page just ships heavier than it needs to. What tips it to *request changes* rather than a "nit, follow-up welcome": this is the **landing-page hero**, so it's almost certainly the LCP element. A quarter-megabyte PNG blocking largest-contentful-paint is the single highest-leverage byte reduction on the page, and it costs one re-encode. Fix it in this PR while the asset is already in the diff; don't open a ticket that ages out. One caveat on the receipts: the finding reports **bytes only, no dimensions** — compare `crime_00036`, where the detector did surface `32 × 32 px`. So I can't tell from the scan whether this is a 4000px export being downscaled in CSS or a correctly-sized image that's just badly encoded. Check the intrinsic size before re-exporting; it changes which half of the fix does the work. ## The transformation to ask for **Dimensions — target the visible render box, cap at 2× DPR.** A full-bleed hero typically renders in a ~1280–1440 CSS-px-wide box. Export at 2× that and stop: | Variant | Use | |---|---| | 1600w | 1× desktop, 2× tablet | | 2560w | 2× desktop / retina | | 800w | mobile | Wire them through `srcset` + `sizes` so phones don't download the desktop asset. Anything beyond 2560w is invisible pixels — 3× DPR is indistinguishable from 2× at hero viewing distance and costs real bytes. If the source turns out to be 3000px+, the downscale alone recovers most of the 254 KB before any format change. **Format — AVIF first, WebP fallback, in a ``.** ```html ``` AVIF is the right primary here specifically because it's a *hero*: heroes are large, photographic or gradient-heavy, and AVIF's main win over WebP is exactly that regime — roughly 20–30% smaller at matched perceptual quality, and materially better at suppressing banding across the wide smooth gradients heroes tend to have. WebP's lossy encoder is VP8-derived and blocks up on gradients at the quality levels where AVIF still looks clean. Why keep WebP rather than going AVIF-only: AVIF encoding is slow (a build-time cost, not a runtime one, so it doesn't matter much) but support gaps are real on older Safari and long-tail Android WebViews. `` makes the fallback free — the browser picks one, downloads one. Keeping PNG in the chain is only worth it if the hero needs alpha *and* you have evidence of traffic from browsers that support neither, which in practice you don't. **Budget to hold it to:** ≤100 KB for the largest variant, and ~40–60 KB is achievable at 1600w AVIF q45–55 for a typical photographic hero. That's a 4–6× reduction from 253.9 KB. Add it to a CI size budget so the next hero doesn't re-litigate this. **One escape hatch worth checking first:** if the "hero banner" is flat-colour artwork, a gradient, or mostly typography, the correct fix isn't a re-encode at all — it's a CSS gradient or an SVG, and the asset drops to near zero. The suggested action calls this out too. Worth thirty seconds of looking at the image before you reach for the encoder. ## Scope note The other 36 findings in this scan are pre-existing and not this PR's problem — including the two genuinely higher-severity asset crimes (`crime_00032`, an SVG with 2 embedded base64 rasters, severity **high**; `crime_00036`, a 32×32 PNG that should be an SVG icon). Don't gate this PR on them, but they're better cleanup candidates than the hero if someone's looking for asset work to do next.
